Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being reminded of the event by others
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

vignette: The violence had not begun with a sentence or a verdict, but with the sudden closing of a metal door and the heavy tread of boots on concrete. For three days, Mateo was kept in a room where the only certainty was the sound of keys turning and the smell of sweat and polished leather. When the door opened, men in dark uniforms stepped through, their movements synchronized, their voices stripped of warmth. They did not ask his name. They only demonstrated that they could end him at any moment, that the space around him was entirely theirs to control. The vehicle that brought him there was a black sedan, windowless, engine purring with a low, mechanical hum that seemed to vibrate in his teeth. He never saw the driver's face, only the way the car idled outside the gate, waiting. When Mateo returned to the United States, the silence of his own apartment felt heavier than the cell. He had come to believe that safety was an illusion he had to actively enforce. Every evening, long after the streets grew quiet, he would lie awake and press his ear against the drywall, listening for footsteps. He would rise, walk to the front door, check the deadbolt, then move to the windows, pressing his forehead against the cool glass until his breathing slowed. He told himself this was how he stayed alive. During the day, he worked as a maid for a family in a suburban residence that required him to clean both the service areas and the main living spaces. The house kept him moving, but it also placed him in rooms where a television might be left running or a resident's car sat in the driveway. When the screen showed news footage of detention centers or prison breaks, Mateo would mute it immediately, his chest tightening. He was certain that watching such things would pull him back into that concrete room. When the engine of a passing car matched that low, windowless purr, he would step out of the kitchen and stand by the back door, hands braced against the frame, waiting until the sound faded. He had learned to steer clear of anyone who wore a uniform, whether it was a postal worker, a building security guard, or a supervisor in a crisp shirt with a badge. At work, he took routes through alleys and back stairwells to avoid encounters. When residents or coworkers mentioned the past, asking how he was coping or bringing up the events he had survived, Mateo would grow quiet and change the subject, or simply stop returning calls. He found that speaking about it did not loosen the knot in his stomach; it only made the room feel smaller. Instead, he smoked. He kept a pack tucked into his cleaning cart, lighting one while he wiped down counters or folded linens, watching the smoke curl upward. He did not know if it helped or merely delayed the shaking. The world had become a place of sudden approaches. In the grocery store, he would cross the aisle when a stranger walked too close. At the job site, if a homeowner reached out to hand him a key or adjust his sleeve, Mateo would flinch, pulling his arm back as though struck, his breath catching in a sharp gasp. He did not think it was aggression that frightened him; he thought it was unpredictability. He had come to believe that kindness could turn to threat in a heartbeat, just as it had before. Even when he felt a moment of relief-a joke from a coworker, the success of a difficult scrub-he would find himself waiting for the other shoe to drop. Happiness felt like a mismatch, something he did not know how to hold without feeling exposed. By the time he called the community health clinic, Mateo had not slept through the night in fourteen months. He was tired of checking locks three times, tired of the way his heart hammered when the elevator dinged, tired of the distance he had put between himself and the few people who still tried to reach him. He wanted to work without bracing for a door to open. He wanted to stop waiting for the car outside his building to sound like the one that had taken him. What he hoped for, when he finally dialed the number, was simply to learn how to let his own house be his own again.
